n: This verse closes the previous discussion: follow Paul’s example of putting others first, just as he follows Christ’s example.

f.g: Greek mimetai — imitators.

n: Paul commends the saints for remembering him and holding to the teachings and practices he passed on to them.

f.g: Here, traditions or teachings handed down.

n: Paul sets out an order of headship: Christ is head of man, man of woman, and God the Father of Christ. Even Christ, though divine, honors His Father’s authority.

f.w: the head of Christ is God

f.g: Can mean authority, source, or the one who represents another.

n: In Corinth’s culture, a man praying or prophesying in worship with his head covered brought shame on his head — and on Christ.

f.g: Speaking by inspiration to others.

n: A woman praying or prophesying uncovered would shame her head. In that culture, a woman uncovered in public could look as disgraceful as one whose head was shaved. Note that women did pray and prophesy in worship.

f.w: all one as if she were shaven
f.g: Equally shameful as a shaved head, which was a sign of disgrace in that society.

n: Paul argues: if a woman won’t cover her head, she might as well cut her hair off. Since that would be shameful, she should be covered.

f.g: Hair cut short.

n: Man reflects God’s image and glory; woman is the glory of man. Paul draws on the creation account to support the custom.

f.w: the image and glory of God

n: In the creation story, the woman was made from the man.
And she was created as a partner for the man.
So a woman should wear a sign of authority on her head, “because of the angels” — perhaps because angels attend worship. The exact meaning is uncertain.

f.g: A symbol of authority — perhaps her own authority to pray and prophesy.
The meaning is debated; possibly angels as witnesses of proper order in worship.

n: But in the Lord, man and woman are not independent of each other. Neither is complete without the other — a core truth of eternal marriage.

f.w: neither is the man without the woman

n: Just as the first woman came from man, every man since has been born of a woman. And all of it comes from God.
Judge for yourselves whether it is proper for a woman to pray publicly uncovered in that setting.

f.g: Proper, fitting.

n: Paul appeals to common sense of his culture: long hair on a man was seen as disgraceful.

f.g: The natural order, or common custom accepted as natural.

n: But long hair is a woman’s glory, given her as a natural covering.

f.g: Something wrapped around, like a veil or mantle.

n: If anyone wants to argue, Paul says the churches have no other practice. These were customs for that time and place.

f.g: Argumentative, quarrelsome.

n: Now Paul gives no praise: their worship gatherings were doing more harm than good.

f.w: not for the better, but for the worse
f.g: Their meetings were making things worse.

n: He hears that when they meet as a congregation, they split into factions — and he partly believes it.
Divisions do serve one purpose: they reveal who is genuinely faithful.

f.g: Here, factions or parties, not necessarily false doctrine.
Tested and proven genuine.

n: Early Christians ate a shared meal with the sacrament. But the way the Corinthians did it, it was no longer truly the Lord’s Supper.

f.g: The sacrament, often celebrated as part of a shared meal (later called the love feast).

n: Wealthier members ate their own food first, while poorer members — who arrived after work — went hungry. Some even got drunk.

f.w: one is hungry, and another is drunken
f.g: A painful picture of class divisions at a sacred meal.

n: If you just want a meal, eat at home! Paul asks whether they despise God’s Church and humiliate the poor. He certainly cannot praise this.
Paul passes on what he received from the Lord: the night Jesus was betrayed, He took bread. This is one of the earliest written accounts of the Last Supper.

f.w: the same night in which he was betrayed

n: Jesus gave thanks, broke the bread, and said it was His body broken for them, to be eaten in remembrance of Him. Remembering Him is the heart of the sacrament.
After supper He took the cup, calling it the new covenant in His blood, and asked them to drink it in remembrance of Him.

f.g: New covenant.

n: Each time we take the sacrament, we proclaim Christ’s death and look forward to His return.
So anyone who takes the sacrament in an unworthy, careless way sins against the Lord’s body and blood.

f.g: In an unworthy manner — irreverently, or without repenting.

n: Each person should examine himself before partaking — reflecting honestly and repenting.
Those who partake carelessly, not recognizing the sacred meaning of the Lord’s body — including His body, the Church — bring judgment on themselves.

f.g: Here, judgment or condemnation.
Recognizing, distinguishing.

n: Paul links this to the illness and even deaths among them.

f.g: A gentle way of saying die.

n: If we honestly judged ourselves, we wouldn’t need to come under God’s judgment.
Even when the Lord disciplines us, it is loving correction to keep us from being condemned with the world.
So when you meet to eat together, wait for each other.

f.g: Wait so all can share together.

n: If you’re hungry, eat at home, so your gatherings don’t bring judgment on you. Paul will address other matters in person.

f.g: Arrange, regulate.
